source_refs.note: Chapter 6 exercise (PDF 167-169, printed 164-166), solved: the flowchart activity, each MCQ with its key worked out from the chapter (the book prints no key), and model answers to the short, long and inquisitive questions.

blocks.prompt:
From the given flowchart, build a paragraph that can describe a comparison between photosynthesis and respiration in terms of reactants and products of major steps.
[The printed flowchart: a chloroplast (left) in which sunlight falls on PS-II and PS-I; NADP and ADP go to the photosystems and NADPH and ATP come out to the Calvin cycle; CO₂ enters the Calvin cycle, which gives glucose. Glucose gives pyruvic acid (with ATP), which enters the Krebs cycle in a mitochondrion (right); the Krebs cycle gives ATP and CO₂ (arrow back to the Calvin cycle) and NADH; NAD and NADH link it to the electron transport chain, which gives ATP and heat. O₂ passes from the photosystems to the electron transport chain, and H₂O from the electron transport chain back to the photosystems.]
blocks.explanation: Photosynthesis and respiration are opposite but linked processes: the products of one are the reactants of the other. Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplast. In its light-dependent reactions, sunlight is absorbed by PS-II and PS-I; water is split and oxygen is released, while NADP and ADP are changed into NADPH and ATP. In the Calvin cycle (light-independent reactions) carbon dioxide is reduced, using this ATP and NADPH, to make glucose; NADP and ADP return to the photosystems. Respiration begins where photosynthesis ends: glucose is broken down in glycolysis to pyruvic acid, giving a little ATP. Pyruvic acid enters the mitochondrion, where the Krebs cycle oxidizes it completely, releasing carbon dioxide (which the Calvin cycle can use again), some ATP and NADH. In the electron transport chain NADH passes its electrons to oxygen, which forms water; most of the ATP is made here and some energy is lost as heat. So photosynthesis uses CO₂, H₂O and light energy and produces glucose and O₂ (an energy-capturing, reduction process), while respiration uses glucose and O₂ and produces CO₂, H₂O and energy as ATP (an energy-releasing, oxidation process).

blocks.prompt: 1- What main process occurs during the dark reaction of photosynthesis?
blocks.explanation: In the dark (light-independent) reactions CO₂ is reduced to sugar: hydrogen from NADPH and energy from ATP are added to it in the Calvin cycle. Oxygen release, light absorption and ATP formation belong to the light-dependent reactions.

blocks.prompt: 2- What is TRUE about glycolysis?

options.text: It takes place only in aerobic respiration
It takes place in the mitochondrion
It reduces 2 molecules of NAD+ for every glucose molecule processed

blocks.explanation: In glycolysis each of the two G3P molecules gives two hydrogen atoms to NAD⁺, so 2NAD⁺ → 2NADH per glucose. Glycolysis makes ATP (net 2), occurs in both aerobic and anaerobic respiration, and takes place in the cytosol.

blocks.prompt: 3- Which of the following are produced by the reactions that occur in the thylakoid and consumed by the reactions that occur in the stroma?
blocks.explanation: The light-dependent reactions on the thylakoid membranes make ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle in the stroma uses them to reduce CO₂ to sugar. NADP⁺ and ADP go the other way.

blocks.prompt: 4- When deprived of oxygen, yeast cells obtain energy by fermentation, producing CO2, ATP and;
blocks.explanation: Yeast carries out alcoholic fermentation: pyruvic acid is changed into ethyl alcohol (C₂H₅OH) and CO₂. Lactic acid fermentation (no CO₂) occurs in muscle cells.

blocks.prompt: 5- Conversion of Glucose 6-phosphate into Fructose 6-phosphate is;
blocks.explanation: In step 2 of glycolysis glucose 6-phosphate is converted into its isomer fructose 6-phosphate (same formula, different arrangement), catalysed by an isomerase.

blocks.prompt: 6- In which of the following conversions, ATP is produced?

options.text: Alpha ketoglutaric acid into succinyl CoA

blocks.explanation: The bond between succinic acid and CoA is a high-energy linkage; when succinyl-CoA splits into CoA and succinic acid, the energy released makes one ATP. The other steps give NADH, FADH₂ or add water.

blocks.prompt: 7- In electron transport chain, FADH:H produces how many ATPs?
blocks.explanation: FADH₂ passes its electrons to coenzyme Q, after the first ATP-making step, so its oxidation produces two ATP (NADH gives three).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: "FADH:H" is printed for the reduced coenzyme; it should read FADH₂.

blocks.prompt: 8- Which of these is CO₂ acceptor during photosynthesis?
blocks.explanation: In carbon fixation Rubisco combines CO₂ with the five-carbon sugar ribulose biphosphate (RuBP), giving 3-phosphoglyceric acid. (In C-4 plants the first acceptor is phosphoenol pyruvic acid, which is not an option.)

blocks.prompt: 9- Which of the following takes the electrons lost by Photosystem I on absorption of light energy?
blocks.explanation: The excited electrons of P700 go to the primary electron acceptor of PS-I and are then received by ferredoxin (Fd), which passes them through NADP reductase to NADP⁺. Plastocyanin brings electrons to PS-I from PS-II.

blocks.prompt: 10- Photosystem-II makes up the electrons lost due to light excitation by taking up the electrons released from,
blocks.explanation: The electron hole in P680 of PS-II is filled by electrons from water: water splits into 2H⁺, an oxygen atom and 2 electrons (photolysis).

blocks.prompt: 1- Differentiate between action spectrum and absorption spectrum.
blocks.explanation: The absorption spectrum shows how much light a pigment absorbs; the action spectrum shows how effective each wavelength is in photosynthesis. The two coincide.

rows: Graph of the rate of photosynthesis at different wavelengths
Graph of the different wavelengths absorbed by a pigment
Measured as oxygen given out by the plant in each colour of light
Measured as light absorbed by an extracted pigment
Shows the effectiveness of each wavelength for photosynthesis
Shows which wavelengths each pigment absorbs
First made by T. W. Engelmann (1883) on Spirogyra
Chlorophylls absorb most at 430 nm (blue) and 670 nm (red)

blocks.prompt: 2- How is photosynthesis a redox reaction?
blocks.explanation:
6CO₂ + 12H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O
Water is oxidized: it loses electrons and hydrogen ions and gives oxygen. CO₂ is reduced: electrons and hydrogen ions are added to it to form sugar. Oxidation and reduction go hand in hand, so photosynthesis is a redox process.

blocks.prompt: 3- Which molecule contributes Oxygen in glucose? Water or carbon dioxide!
blocks.explanation: Carbon dioxide. In the ¹⁸O experiment, plants given H₂¹⁸O released ¹⁸O₂, while plants given C¹⁸O₂ released normal O₂. So the O₂ released comes from water, and the oxygen built into glucose comes from CO₂.

blocks.prompt: 4- State the role of CO₂ in photosynthesis.
blocks.explanation: CO₂ is the source of carbon for making sugars. It enters leaves through stomata and dissolves in the water of mesophyll cell walls; in the Calvin cycle Rubisco fixes it with RuBP, and it is reduced to sugar using ATP and NADPH.

blocks.prompt: 5- Define electron transport chain.
blocks.explanation: The electron transport chain is a series of electron carriers (in the inner mitochondrial membrane, or the thylakoid membrane) that pass electrons from one to the next by redox reactions; in respiration they go from NADH and FADH₂ to oxygen, forming water. The energy released is used to make ATP by chemiosmosis.

blocks.prompt: 6- What do you mean by glycolysis?
blocks.explanation: Glycolysis is the breakdown of one glucose molecule (6C) into two molecules of pyruvic acid (3C) by a series of enzyme-catalysed steps in the cytosol. It needs no oxygen, occurs in both aerobic and anaerobic respiration, and gives a net 2 ATP and 2 NADH.

blocks.prompt: 7- What is the main structural difference between chlorophyll-a and chlorophyll-b?
blocks.explanation: Both have a porphyrin head (four pyrrole rings around a Mg atom) and a long hydrocarbon tail. The difference is on the second pyrrole ring: chlorophyll-a has a methyl group (CH₃), chlorophyll-b has an aldehyde group (CHO) at the same spot.

blocks.prompt: 8- How can a cell synthesize ATP through substrate-level phosphorylation?
blocks.explanation:
An enzyme transfers a phosphate group directly from an organic substrate molecule to ADP, forming ATP and a new organic molecule; no membrane or electron transport chain is involved.
Example: in the last step of glycolysis, phosphoenol pyruvic acid + ADP → pyruvic acid + ATP.

blocks.prompt: 9- Can pyruvic acid enter Krebs cycle as such? If not, what changes are made to it before Krebs cycle?
blocks.explanation:
No. In pyruvic acid oxidation (in the mitochondrion):
1. CO₂ is removed, giving acetaldehyde.
2. Acetaldehyde is oxidized to an acetyl group; NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH.
3. The acetyl group combines with coenzyme A to form acetyl-CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle.

blocks.prompt: 10- Differentiate between C-3 and C-4 photosynthesis.
blocks.explanation: C-3 plants fix CO₂ only by the Calvin cycle; C-4 plants first fix it into a four-carbon acid and then run the Calvin cycle, which reduces photorespiration.

rows: First product is the 3-carbon 3-phosphoglyceric acid
First product is the 4-carbon oxaloacetic acid
CO₂ acceptor: RuBP (by Rubisco)
First CO₂ acceptor: phosphoenol pyruvic acid (3C) in mesophyll cells
Calvin cycle runs in mesophyll cells
Calvin cycle runs mainly in bundle-sheath cells
High photorespiration; loses 25-50% of fixed carbon in hot climates
Little photorespiration because CO₂ is concentrated in bundle-sheath cells
Lower energy cost
About double energy cost per glucose (extra ATP)
Examples: most plants (wheat, rice)
Examples: corn, sugarcane, sorghum

blocks.prompt: 1- What are photosynthetic pigments and what role they play in the absorption and conversion of light energy?
blocks.explanation:
Photosynthetic pigments are coloured molecules in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts that capture the light energy needed for photosynthesis: chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, carotenoids (carotenes and xanthophylls) and, in red algae and cyanobacteria, phycobilins.
Absorption of light:
- Light behaves as a stream of particles called photons; a pigment molecule absorbs one photon at a time.
- Different pigments absorb different wavelengths. Chlorophylls absorb mainly violet-blue and orange-red light (peaks at 430 nm and 670 nm) and reflect green; carotenoids absorb in the blue-green region.
- Accessory pigments (chlorophyll b, carotenoids, phycobilins) widen the range of light used and pass their energy on to chlorophyll a. Carotenoids also protect the photosynthetic apparatus from damage by excess light.
Conversion of light energy:
- When a pigment absorbs a photon, its electrons move to a higher energy level and it becomes excited.
- In a photosystem, the antenna pigments pass this excitation energy to chlorophyll a of the reaction centre (P680 or P700).
- The reaction centre passes high-energy electrons to the primary electron acceptor and then along the electron transport chain.
- Their energy is used to make ATP (photophosphorylation by chemiosmosis) and NADPH; the lost electrons of P680 are replaced from water, releasing O₂.
- ATP and NADPH are then used in the Calvin cycle to store the energy as C-H bonds of sugar. Thus light energy becomes chemical energy.

blocks.prompt: 2- How are the absorption spectra of chlorophyll 'a' and 'b' different?
blocks.explanation: Both chlorophylls absorb mainly violet-blue and orange-red light and absorb least in the green (green is reflected), but their peaks are at slightly different wavelengths. Some wavelengths not absorbed by chlorophyll a are very effectively absorbed by chlorophyll b and vice versa, which increases the range of light absorbed.

rows: Main pigment; found in the reaction centres (P680, P700)
Accessory pigment; passes absorbed energy to chlorophyll a
Blue peak at a shorter wavelength, about 430 nm (beyond the chapter: exact values)
Blue peak shifted to a longer wavelength, about 450-455 nm (beyond the chapter)
Red peak at a longer wavelength, about 660-670 nm
Red peak shifted to a shorter wavelength, about 640-645 nm (beyond the chapter)
Absorbs some wavelengths that chlorophyll b misses
Absorbs some wavelengths that chlorophyll a misses, widening the range
Has a methyl group (CH₃) on the second pyrrole ring
Has an aldehyde group (CHO) at the same place

blocks.prompt: 3- Describe and illustrate how photosynthetic pigments are organized in thylakoid membrane?
blocks.explanation:
For efficient absorption and use of light, photosynthetic pigments are organized into clusters called photosystems, embedded in the thylakoid membranes of the grana. Each photosystem contains pigments and carriers of the electron transport chain and has two parts:
1. Antenna complex (light-gathering): many pigment molecules (chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, carotenoids) bound to proteins; they capture light and pass the excitation energy from molecule to molecule towards the reaction centre.
2. Reaction centre: one or more special chlorophyll a molecules that pass high-energy electrons to a primary electron acceptor, which hands them on to the electron transport chain.
Two photosystems (named in order of discovery):
- Photosystem I (PS-I): reaction centre P700, absorbs best light of 700 nm.
- Photosystem II (PS-II): reaction centre P680, absorbs best light of 680 nm.
Illustration (Fig. 5.7): draw a section of the thylakoid membrane (two parallel lines, stroma above, lumen below). Inside it draw a large oval photosystem: many small green dots (pigment molecules) form the antenna complex; arrows of light (photons) strike them; zig-zag arrows show energy passing from pigment to pigment to a central pair of chlorophyll a labelled "reaction centre (P680/P700)"; from it an arrow of an electron (e⁻) goes to a box labelled "primary electron acceptor", and from there to the electron transport chain. Draw PS-II and PS-I side by side in the membrane, joined by the carriers PQ, cytochrome complex and PC.

blocks.prompt: 4- Describe how the role of water in photosynthesis can be explained through experiment.
blocks.explanation:
Role of water: water is the source of hydrogen for reducing CO₂, and the oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from water.
Hypothesis: in the 1930s Van Niel, working on photosynthetic bacteria that make carbohydrate from CO₂ without releasing oxygen, hypothesized that plants split water as a source of hydrogen and release oxygen as a by-product.
Experiment (1940s, isotopic tracer ¹⁸O):
1. Scientists prepared water with heavy oxygen (H₂¹⁸O) and carbon dioxide with heavy oxygen (C¹⁸O₂).
2. Group 1 plants were given H₂¹⁸O and normal CO₂ (C¹⁶O₂).
3. Group 2 plants were given C¹⁸O₂ and normal water (H₂¹⁶O).
4. Both groups carried out photosynthesis, and the oxygen they released was collected and tested.
Result: group 1 released ¹⁸O₂; group 2 released normal oxygen (¹⁶O₂).
Conclusion: the oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from water, not from CO₂. Water is split (photolysis); its hydrogen reduces NADP to NADPH, the reducing power used to reduce CO₂ to sugar. This confirmed Van Niel's hypothesis; water is therefore the main source of atmospheric oxygen.

blocks.prompt: 5- What are the events that capture light and convert it into chemical energy during light dependent reactions?
blocks.explanation:
Key events: absorption of light by pigments, excitation of electrons, and formation of ATP and NADPH. Usually this happens by non-cyclic photophosphorylation, in which both photosystems take part:
1. Absorption of light by PS-II: light raises the energy of antenna chlorophylls; the energy reaches P680, whose two excited electrons pass to the primary electron acceptor of PS-II. An electron "hole" is left in P680, which becomes a strong oxidizing agent.
2. Photolysis of water: water splits into 2H⁺, an oxygen atom (two combine to form O₂) and 2 electrons, which fill the hole in P680.
3. Electron flow from PS-II to PS-I: the electrons pass along an electron transport chain of plastoquinone (PQ), cytochrome complex and plastocyanin (PC). Their energy falls step by step and is used to make ATP by chemiosmosis.
4. Absorption of light by PS-I: P700 is excited; its electrons go to the primary electron acceptor of PS-I, and the electrons coming from PS-II fill the hole in P700.
5. Electron flow from PS-I to NADP⁺: the electrons pass to ferredoxin (Fd); the enzyme NADP reductase transfers them to NADP⁺, which with an H⁺ is reduced to NADPH.
Chemiosmosis: the energy of the electrons pumps H⁺ from the stroma into the lumen; H⁺ flows back through ATP synthase, which joins ADP and Pi to make ATP (photophosphorylation).
The zigzag path of electrons from water through PS-II and PS-I to NADP⁺ is called the Z-scheme. Products: ATP (assimilatory power) and NADPH (reducing power) for the Calvin cycle, and O₂ as a by-product. Thus light energy is converted into chemical energy.

blocks.prompt: 6- Illustrate the cyclic photophosphorylation.
blocks.explanation:
Cyclic photophosphorylation: under certain conditions the photoexcited electrons of PS-I take an alternative cyclic path. Only PS-I is used, not PS-II.
Steps:
1. Light excites P700 of PS-I; its high-energy electrons pass to the primary electron acceptor of PS-I.
2. The electrons go to ferredoxin (Fd) but, instead of going to NADP⁺, they cycle back through the electron transport chain (cytochrome complex and plastocyanin) to P700.
3. As they pass down the chain, their energy pumps H⁺ into the lumen and ATP is made by chemiosmosis.
Result: ATP is produced; there is no production of NADPH and no release of oxygen (water is not split).
When: when the Calvin cycle slows down and NADPH accumulates in the chloroplast; the extra ATP meets the Calvin cycle's need for more ATP than NADPH.
Illustration (Fig. 5.10): draw PS-I with P700 at the bottom left and light arrows on it; an upward arrow of e⁻ to the "primary electron acceptor" high on the energy scale; from it an arrow to "Fd", then a downward arrow through "cytochrome complex" (mark "ATP" formed here) and "PC", ending back at P700, so the arrows make a closed loop. Label "no NADPH, no O₂".

blocks.prompt: 7- Describe light independent reactions of photosynthesis in terms of paragraph and illustrate in terms of Calvin cycle.
blocks.explanation:
Paragraph: Light-independent (dark) reactions are a series of reactions in the stroma of the chloroplast that use carbon from CO₂, energy from ATP and hydrogen from NADPH (both made in the light reactions) to build energy-rich sugar. They can occur in light or darkness as long as ATP and NADPH are available. Their details were worked out by Melvin Calvin and colleagues (Nobel Prize 1961), so they are called the Calvin cycle; because the first product has three carbons, it is also called the C-3 pathway. The cycle has three phases:
1. Carbon fixation: Rubisco (ribulose biphosphate carboxylase, probably the most abundant protein on Earth) combines 3 CO₂ with 3 molecules of the five-carbon ribulose biphosphate (RuBP), forming 6 molecules of 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA).
2. Reduction: 6 ATP add phosphate groups, changing 3-PGA into 1,3-biphosphoglyceric acid; 6 NADPH then reduce it to 6 glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (G3P), and the phosphates are removed. One G3P leaves the cycle; two G3P combine to make glucose and other carbohydrates.
3. Regeneration of RuBP: the other 5 G3P are rearranged into 3 ribulose phosphate (RuP); 3 ATP add a phosphate to each, giving 3 RuBP, which accept CO₂ again.
So for 3 CO₂ fixed: 9 ATP and 6 NADPH are used and 1 G3P is gained; one glucose needs 6 turns of CO₂ fixation (18 ATP, 12 NADPH).
Illustration (Fig. 5.12): draw a large circle with three arrows clockwise. At the top write "3 CO₂ enter" with "Rubisco"; next to it "3 RuBP (5C)" joining to give "6 3-PGA (3C)" (phase 1: carbon fixation). Down the right side: "6 ATP → 6 ADP" and "6 NADPH → 6 NADP⁺" giving "6 G3P" (phase 2: reduction); an arrow out of the circle "1 G3P → glucose and other carbohydrates". Up the left side: "5 G3P" with "3 ATP → 3 ADP" back to "3 RuBP" (phase 3: regeneration).

blocks.prompt: 8- What happens with glucose in anaerobic respiration and how different organisms modify the end products?
blocks.explanation:
Anaerobic respiration (fermentation) occurs without oxygen in many microorganisms, some cells of higher plants and vertebrate muscle cells. Glucose is not completely oxidized:
1. Glycolysis: glucose is split into 2 pyruvic acid (C₃H₄O₃) in the cytosol, giving a net 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
2. Pyruvic acid is then reduced by NADH (this regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue) into end products that still contain much energy.
End products differ in different organisms:
- Alcoholic fermentation: in yeast and some bacteria, pyruvic acid is converted into ethyl alcohol (C₂H₅OH) and CO₂: 2C₃H₄O₃ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂.
- Lactic acid fermentation: in muscle cells of humans and other animals (during extreme activity when oxygen cannot be supplied fast enough) and in many bacteria, pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid (C₃H₆O₃), with no CO₂ released.
Energy yield: only 2 ATP per glucose (about 2% of the energy of glucose; 14.6 kcal), far less than the 36 ATP of aerobic respiration.

blocks.prompt: 9- How is glucose broken down to pyruvic acid in glycolysis?
blocks.explanation:
Glycolysis takes place in the cytosol; each step is catalysed by a specific enzyme, and ATP and NAD⁺ are needed. It has two phases.
Preparatory phase (energy is spent and glucose is split):
1. A phosphate from ATP is transferred to glucose → glucose 6-phosphate.
2. Glucose 6-phosphate is converted into its isomer → fructose 6-phosphate.
3. A second ATP adds another phosphate → fructose 1,6-biphosphate.
4. Fructose 1,6-biphosphate splits into two 3-carbon molecules, glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (G3P) and dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DAP); these interconvert, giving 2 G3P.
Oxidative phase (for each G3P, so everything happens twice):
5. G3P is oxidized: 2 hydrogen atoms go to NAD⁺ (→ NADH) and an inorganic phosphate is added → 1,3-biphosphoglyceric acid (1,3-BPGA).
6. A phosphate is transferred from 1,3-BPGA to ADP → ATP + 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA).
7. 3-PGA is converted to 2-phosphoglyceric acid (2-PGA).
8. 2-PGA loses water → phosphoenol pyruvic acid (PEP).
9. PEP gives its phosphate to ADP → ATP + pyruvic acid.
Balance per glucose: 2 ATP used, 4 ATP made (by substrate-level phosphorylation) = net 2 ATP; 2 NADH; 2 pyruvic acid.
Glucose + 2ADP + 2Pi + 2NAD⁺ → 2 pyruvic acid + 2ATP + 2NADH + 2H⁺

blocks.prompt: 10- Describe how Krebs cycle is the completion of the oxidation of glycolytic products.
blocks.explanation:
Glycolysis oxidizes glucose only partly: its products, 2 pyruvic acid, still hold most of the energy. In the mitochondrion they are oxidized completely to CO₂.
Pyruvic acid oxidation (link step, per pyruvic acid): CO₂ is removed (→ acetaldehyde); oxidation gives an acetyl group and NADH; the acetyl group joins coenzyme A → acetyl-CoA.
Krebs (citric acid) cycle, worked out by Sir Hans Krebs, in the mitochondrion:
1. Acetyl group (2C) + oxaloacetic acid (4C) → citric acid (6C); CoA is released.
2. Citric acid is decarboxylated (CO₂ released) and oxidized (NAD⁺ → NADH) → alpha-ketoglutaric acid (5C).
3. Alpha-ketoglutaric acid is again oxidized and decarboxylated (CO₂, NADH) → succinic acid (4C), which joins CoA → succinyl-CoA.
4. Succinyl-CoA splits into CoA and succinic acid; the energy of this high-energy bond makes 1 ATP.
5. Succinic acid is oxidized to fumaric acid; the hydrogens reduce FAD → FADH₂.
6. Water is added to fumaric acid → malic acid.
7. Malic acid is oxidized (NAD⁺ → NADH) → oxaloacetic acid, which is free to accept another acetyl-CoA.
Why it completes the oxidation: per glucose (two turns), the 6 carbons of glucose all leave as CO₂ (2 in pyruvic acid oxidation, 4 in the Krebs cycle), and all the hydrogen and electrons are taken by coenzymes: 8 NADH and 2 FADH₂ (plus 2 NADH from glycolysis) and 2 ATP. These reduced coenzymes pass their electrons to the electron transport chain, where most ATP is made and oxygen accepts the electrons to form water.

blocks.prompt: 11- Explain the passage of electron through electron transport chain.
blocks.explanation:
The electron transport chain of respiration is built into the inner membrane of the mitochondrion. Electrons come from the reduced coenzymes NADH and FADH₂ made in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle.
Pathway of electrons (Fig. 5.18):
1. NADH is oxidized (→ NAD⁺) and its electrons are taken by coenzyme Q (CoQ). FADH₂ is oxidized (→ FAD) and its electrons also go to CoQ.
2. Reduced CoQ passes the electrons to cytochrome b.
3. Cytochrome b passes them to cytochrome c.
4. Cytochrome c passes them to the cytochrome a complex (cytochromes a and a₃).
5. This complex passes them to an atom of oxygen at the end of the chain; the oxygen takes two electrons and two H⁺ to form water: ½O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂O.
Redox: each carrier is reduced when it gains electrons and oxidized when it passes them on. Electrons lose energy at each step.
Use of the energy: the energy released pumps H⁺ from the matrix to the inter-membrane space; H⁺ flows back through ATP synthase, which makes ATP (chemiosmosis). One NADH gives 3 ATP; one FADH₂ gives 2 ATP. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor; without it the chain stops.

blocks.prompt: 12- Define chemiosmosis. How would you relate it with electron transport chain?
blocks.explanation:
Chemiosmosis is the mechanism in which membranes couple the redox reactions of an electron transport chain with the synthesis of ATP, using a gradient of H⁺ ions.
Relation with the electron transport chain:
1. As electrons pass from carrier to carrier in the ETC (redox reactions), they lose energy.
2. This energy is used to actively transport H⁺ across the membrane: in mitochondria from the matrix to the inter-membrane space; in chloroplasts from the stroma into the thylakoid lumen.
3. H⁺ accumulates on one side; the H⁺ gradient stores potential energy.
4. H⁺ diffuses back down its gradient through a special membrane protein, the enzyme ATP synthase.
5. The flow of H⁺ drives ATP synthase to join ADP and Pi into ATP.
So the ETC builds the H⁺ gradient and chemiosmosis uses it to make ATP; without the ETC there is no gradient and no ATP. The same mechanism makes ATP in both mitochondria (oxidative phosphorylation) and chloroplasts (photophosphorylation).

blocks.prompt: 13- Through which ways proteins and fats enter cellular respiration?
blocks.explanation:
Proteins:
- They are first digested (hydrolysed) into amino acids; a cell uses most amino acids to make its own proteins.
- Extra amino acids are de-aminated (the amino group is removed).
- The remaining carbon parts are converted into pyruvic acid, acetyl-CoA or organic acids of the Krebs cycle, and their energy is converted to ATP.
Fats (lipids):
- They are excellent fuel because they have many C-H bonds.
- They are first hydrolysed into glycerol and fatty acids.
- Glycerol is converted into glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (G3P) and enters glycolysis.
- Fatty acids are changed into acetyl-CoA and enter the Krebs cycle.
Thus proteins and fats enter respiration at glycolysis, pyruvic acid, acetyl-CoA or the Krebs cycle and are oxidized like glucose.

blocks.prompt: 14- Define photorespiration and present it in proving that "photosynthesis is not perfect".
blocks.explanation:
Photorespiration: the respiratory activity of green cells in the presence of light that uses O₂ and releases CO₂ (like aerobic respiration) but produces no ATP.
Mechanism: when CO₂ is low and O₂ is high in leaf cells, Rubisco adds O₂ to RuBP instead of CO₂. RuBP breaks into one phosphoglycerate and one phosphoglycolate (2C). Phosphoglycolate → glycolate, which moves to a peroxisome and is changed to glyoxylate using O₂ (toxic H₂O₂ is also formed). Glyoxylate → glycine, which goes to a mitochondrion; two glycines form one serine and CO₂ is released. Serine returns to the peroxisome → glycerate, which goes back to the chloroplast as phosphoglycerate and re-enters the Calvin cycle.
Why this proves that photosynthesis is not perfect:
1. The key enzyme Rubisco is not specific: CO₂ and O₂ compete for the same active site, so it wastes RuBP on oxygen.
2. Carbon already fixed is lost as CO₂: C-3 plants lose 25-50% of their fixed carbon, reducing yields.
3. It uses energy (ATP and NADPH spent to recycle the products) but produces no ATP and no sugar.
4. It produces toxic hydrogen peroxide.
5. It gets worse at high temperature (above 28 °C in the tropics), when Rubisco's oxidative activity rises more than its carbon-fixing activity.
6. It is a leftover of evolution: Rubisco evolved when the atmosphere had little O₂; after O₂ accumulated, the competition began.
Plants had to evolve extra pathways (C-4 photosynthesis, CAM) to reduce this loss, showing that the basic C-3 process is imperfect.

blocks.prompt: 15- What are the effects of temperature on the oxidative activity of Rubisco?
blocks.explanation:
Rubisco has two activities: carboxylase (adds CO₂ to RuBP, carbon fixation) and oxygenase (adds O₂ to RuBP, photorespiration).
Effects of temperature:
1. As temperature rises, the oxidative (oxygenase) activity of Rubisco increases more than its carbon-fixing activity, so the rate of photorespiration rises.
2. In tropical climates, especially where temperatures are often above 28 °C, photorespiration becomes a severe problem and has a major negative impact on agricultural yields.
3. More fixed carbon is lost: C-3 plants may lose 25-50% (in hot climates more than half) of the carbon they fix.
4. (Beyond the chapter) In hot, dry weather stomata close to save water, so CO₂ in the leaf falls and O₂ from photosynthesis builds up; also CO₂ becomes less soluble than O₂ at higher temperatures. Both favour the oxygenase reaction.
5. At lower temperatures the carboxylase activity dominates and photorespiration is small.
This is why C-4 and CAM plants, which concentrate CO₂ around Rubisco, are common in hot climates.

blocks.prompt: 16- How is the process of C4 photosynthesis an adaptation to deal with the problem of photorespiration?
blocks.explanation:
Problem: in hot climates, when CO₂ in the leaf falls and O₂ rises, Rubisco fixes O₂ instead of CO₂ and C-3 plants lose much fixed carbon by photorespiration.
C-4 photosynthesis (grasses such as corn, sugarcane and sorghum, and about two dozen other plant groups) solves it by concentrating CO₂ around Rubisco:
1. Leaf structure: mesophyll cells have fewer air spaces; the Calvin cycle enzymes are mainly in bundle-sheath cells, which are impermeable to CO₂.
2. In mesophyll cells, CO₂ is attached to phosphoenol pyruvic acid (3C) to form oxaloacetic acid (4C), the first product (hence C-4). The enzyme here does not fix O₂.
3. Oxaloacetic acid is converted to malic acid (using NADH) and transported to an adjacent bundle-sheath cell.
4. In the bundle-sheath cell, malic acid is broken down to pyruvic acid and CO₂. These cells hold the CO₂, so its concentration rises.
5. With high CO₂, Rubisco runs the Calvin cycle (C-3) instead of photorespiration.
6. Pyruvic acid returns to the mesophyll cell and is changed back to phosphoenol pyruvic acid using ATP.
Thus C-4 plants carry out both C-4 and C-3 pathways, separated in different cells. The cost is almost double the energy per glucose, but in hot climates, where photorespiration would remove more than half of the fixed carbon, it is the best compromise.

blocks.prompt: 1. Why does cellular respiration release energy more efficiently than fermentation?
blocks.explanation:
1. Complete versus incomplete oxidation: aerobic respiration oxidizes glucose completely to CO₂ and H₂O, releasing the energy of all its C-H bonds; fermentation stops after glycolysis and leaves most energy locked in ethanol or lactic acid.
2. Use of NADH: in aerobic respiration NADH and FADH₂ pass electrons through the electron transport chain to oxygen, making most ATP by chemiosmosis (3 per NADH, 2 per FADH₂); in fermentation NADH is used only to reduce pyruvic acid, making no ATP.
3. Oxygen as the final electron acceptor allows the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain to run.
4. Yield: aerobic respiration gives 36 ATP per glucose, fermentation only 2 ATP (about 2% of glucose energy), so aerobic respiration is 18 times more efficient.

blocks.prompt: 2. Why is the conversion of glucose into ATP during cellular respiration considered a more efficient use of energy than burning glucose directly?
blocks.explanation:
1. Burning glucose releases all its energy at once, as heat and light. Cells cannot capture this energy for work, and such a sudden release of heat would damage the cell.
2. In respiration, glucose is oxidized step by step, each step controlled by a specific enzyme at body temperature (37 °C), so energy is released in small amounts.
3. At each step much of the energy is captured: in NADH and FADH₂ and then, through the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis, in ATP (36 ATP per glucose; each ATP bond releases about 7.3 kcal per mole). Only part is lost as heat.
4. ATP is a usable energy currency: it carries energy to wherever work is needed (contraction, active transport, synthesis) and releases it in small amounts.
(Beyond the chapter: complete oxidation of glucose releases about 686 kcal per mole; 36 × 7.3 = 263 kcal is stored in ATP, about 38%, which is high compared with a car engine at about 25%.)

blocks.prompt: 3. Why might a disruption in either photosynthesis or respiration processes affect global carbon and oxygen cycles?
blocks.explanation:
Photosynthesis and respiration are the two halves of the carbon and oxygen cycles: the products of one are the reactants of the other.
- Photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the air and water and releases O₂ (from water): 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O. The oxygen released in photolysis is the main source of atmospheric oxygen.
- Respiration of all organisms uses O₂ and returns CO₂ to the atmosphere: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy.
- Normally the two are balanced, keeping the levels of CO₂ and O₂ in the atmosphere fairly steady.
If photosynthesis is disrupted (deforestation, pollution of oceans and lakes, where most photosynthesis occurs), less CO₂ is removed and less O₂ is produced: CO₂ builds up (beyond the chapter: adding to global warming) and the oxygen supply for aerobic organisms falls; food chains also lose their energy base.
If respiration is disrupted (for example, fewer decomposers), CO₂ return slows, dead organic matter accumulates, and carbon is locked away; plants would then have less CO₂ for photosynthesis.
So any imbalance shifts the amounts of carbon and oxygen in the air, water and living things worldwide.
